Now let me compile the verse-by-verse commentary from the sources I've been able to read.

---

# Leviticus 23:1–22 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Overview of the Passage

The chapter gives the calendar of Israel's appointed holy days. Verses 1–22 cover the weekly Sabbath and the four spring feasts: Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, and the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost). Commentators across traditions agree these feasts are both historical commemorations for Israel and typological "shadows" pointing to Christ and the Church (Colossians 2:16–17).

---

## v. 1: "Then the LORD said to Moses…"

This begins a new section on holy seasons, following earlier legislation about the holiness of the sanctuary, priests, and sacrifices. Ellicott notes the transition: "The regulations about the holiness of the sanctuary and the sacrifices, the holiness of the priests and the people, are now followed by statutes about holy seasons" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)). Gill similarly observes that after laws concerning the purity of people, priests, and sacrifices, God now appoints "various times and seasons, for the more special worship and service of him" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html)).

---

## v. 2: "Speak to the Israelites… 'These are My appointed feasts… sacred assemblies.'"

The Hebrew word translated "feasts" is *mo'ed*, meaning "appointed times" or "set feasts" — not secular banquets but religious assemblies convened at an appointed time and place (Whedon, [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/leviticus-23.html)). The word fundamentally means an appointed meeting. Gill notes the term has "the signification of stated, fixed, appointed times and seasons, and of convening or meeting together at such times" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html)).

David Guzik (Enduring Word) stresses that the major theme in all these feasts is **gratitude** — "for what God has done and what God continues to give." He quotes Adam Clarke: "An ungrateful heart is an unfeeling, unloving, unbelieving, and disobedient heart" ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

These feasts fundamentally belonged to God: "They fundamentally belonged to God, and He gave them to Israel as holy convocations, sacred gatherings" ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

**Denominational note:** Bell's Commentary (Baptist-leaning) highlights that "feasts" here means "nothing to do with eating" (the Day of Atonement was a fast); the Hebrew *mo'ed* means "appointed times," while another word *hag* (used for Unleavened Bread, Pentecost, and Tabernacles) speaks of "special joy and festivity" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cbb/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cbb/leviticus-23.html)).

---

## v. 3: "For six days work may be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest…"

The Sabbath introduces the holy seasons. Ellicott calls it "the most important as well as the oldest of all festivals." During the second Temple period, it was declared that "the Sabbath is in importance equal to the whole law; he who profanes the Sabbath openly is like him who transgresses the whole law" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

**Key distinction — "no work" vs. "no servile work":** Ellicott notes a vital lexical distinction: on the Sabbath and Day of Atonement, *all* work was prohibited. On other festival days (vv. 7, 8, 21), only "servile work" was forbidden — work connected with food preparation was permitted (Exodus 12:16). The Sabbath and Day of Atonement were unique in their absolute work prohibition ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

Gill notes the Sabbath was observed "in all your dwellings" — unlike other feasts kept at the sanctuary, the Sabbath was kept in private houses, synagogues, and wherever Israelites travelled ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html)).

Constable's Notes (Dallas Theological Seminary) observes that the Sabbath was "the heart of the whole system of annual feasts in Israel. The other feasts all related to the central idea of rest that the Sabbath epitomized" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-23.html)).

**The Sabbath question — where Protestant traditions differ:**

- **Reformed / Baptist (majority evangelical view):** Guzik states plainly that "under the New Covenant, no one is under obligation to observe a Sabbath day (Colossians 2:16–17 and Galatians 4:9–11)." The rest Christians enter is "something to experience every day, not just one day a week — the rest of knowing we don't have to work to save ourselves." Jesus fulfilled the Sabbath's purpose; "since the shadow of the Sabbath is fulfilled in Jesus, we are free to keep any particular day — or no day — as a Sabbath after the custom of ancient Israel" ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)). This reflects the classic Reformed understanding that the ceremonial Sabbath has been fulfilled in Christ, though the moral principle of rest and worship remains.

- **Lutheran and some Reformed (the "Christian Sabbath" view):** These traditions historically hold that while the ceremonial aspect is fulfilled, the moral command (one day in seven for rest and worship) continues under the New Covenant, transferred to Sunday (the Lord's Day) in honour of Christ's resurrection. (I was unable to fetch specific LCMS/1517.org pages on this passage, so this is noted as an important tradition difference without attribution to a specific page.)

- **Seventh-day observers:** Some groups (not represented in the fetched sources) maintain the seventh-day (Saturday) Sabbath remains binding.

---

## v. 4: "These are the LORD's appointed feasts, the sacred assemblies you are to proclaim at their appointed times."

This verse introduces the seven annual festivals as distinct from the weekly Sabbath. Ellicott explains: "Because the following are the festivals proper as distinguished from the sabbath… and because they are now enumerated in their regular order, the introductory heading is here repeated" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)). Gill adds that these were "to be proclaimed by the priests with the sound of trumpet" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html)).

Guzik notes that while the Sabbath could be observed anywhere, the other feasts required attendance at the central sanctuary ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

---

## v. 5: "The Passover to the LORD begins at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month."

The first month (Abib/Nisan, roughly March–April). "Twilight" (Hebrew "between the two evenings") was a point of rabbinic debate: the Sadducees understood it as between sunset and dark; the Pharisees understood it as from afternoon until sunset, which allowed the slaughter of the large number of Passover lambs beginning at about 12:30 p.m. (Ellicott, [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

Guzik connects the first Passover (Exodus 12) — where the lamb's blood on doorposts caused the angel of death to "pass over" — to Christ: "Jesus is clearly identified as our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7)… He is the Lamb of God (John 1:29, 1:36), and it is His blood that makes the judgment of God pass over each of us" ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

Jay Sklar (writing at Desiring God, a Reformed/Baptist source) likewise says: "The New Testament writers use the Passover to explain the death of Jesus… It is a fitting metaphor, since Jesus's sacrifice also delivers us from the Lord's judgment (1 Thessalonians 1:10) and leads us out of sin's slavery into adoption as the Lord's children" ([desiringgod.org/articles/israels-calendar-was-a-classroom](https://desiringgod.org/articles/israels-calendar-was-a-classroom)).

---

## v. 6: "On the fifteenth day of the same month begins the Feast of Unleavened Bread… For seven days you must eat unleavened bread."

The Feast of Unleavened Bread ran from Nisan 15 to 21, immediately following Passover. Historically, it commemorated the haste of the Exodus — Israel left Egypt so quickly there was no time for dough to rise (Exodus 12:34, 39). Guzik notes this was "one of the three feasts at which God commanded all the men of Israel to gather before Him yearly (Exodus 23:17)" ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

Spiritually, leaven (yeast) is consistently a picture of sin and corruption — a little leaven influences the whole lump, and leaven "puffs up" as pride does. Gray's Commentary states: "Leaven is the type of evil or moral corruption, and its removal signifies that the redeemed nation must be a holy and separate people" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/leviticus-23.html)). Guzik ties this to 1 Corinthians 5:7–8, where Paul urges believers to "purge out the old leaven" and keep the feast with "the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

---

## vv. 7–8: "On the first day you are to hold a sacred assembly… On the seventh day there shall be a sacred assembly…"

The first and seventh days of Unleavened Bread were "holy convocations" with prohibition of "regular work" (servile work — agricultural or trade labour, but food preparation was permitted). Ellicott defines servile work as "building, pulling down edifices, weaving, reaping, threshing, winnowing, grinding, etc.," while permitted necessary work included "killing beasts, kneading dough, baking bread, boiling, roasting, etc." The penalty for violating this (unlike Sabbath violation, which brought death) was "forty stripes save one" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

Verse 8 requires an offering made by fire for all seven days. Ellicott specifies these were two young bullocks, a ram, seven lambs with grain offerings, and a goat for a sin offering (Numbers 28:19–23), plus voluntary offerings from each individual ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

---

## v. 9: "And the LORD said to Moses…"

A new divine speech formula introduces the Feast of Firstfruits. Ellicott explains: "As the celebration of the sheaf of first-fruits formed no part of the original institution of the Passover (Exodus 12:1–20), and as the omer ritual could not be observed in the wilderness, where there was no sowing of corn, it is here enacted as a prospective part of the feast of unleavened bread, and hence is introduced by a separate formula" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

---

## v. 10: "When you enter the land that I am giving you and you reap its harvest, you are to bring to the priest a sheaf of the firstfruits…"

This command was given prospectively — Israel was still at Sinai, far from Canaan. Guzik notes: "That God gave them the command for the feast was a promise that they would in fact come into the land… God said, *when* you come into the land, and not '*if* you come'" ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

The "sheaf" (Hebrew *omer*) was of barley, the first grain to ripen. Gill explains that the omer was the tenth part of an ephah. The standing corn was reaped with great ceremony by delegates from the Sanhedrin on the evening ending Nisan 15, then brought to the Temple, threshed, parched by fire, ground, and sifted through thirteen sieves before a tenth (an omer) was taken, mixed with oil and frankincense, and presented by the priest ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html)).

---

## v. 11: "And he shall wave the sheaf before the LORD… on the day after the Sabbath."

The waving was "to and fro, backwards and forwards, upwards and downwards, to make an acknowledgment to the Lord of heaven and earth, that the fruits of the earth and the plentiful harvest were of Him" (Gill, [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html)).

**"The day after the Sabbath" — a famous interpretive dispute:** Ellicott recounts the Pharisaic–Sadducean debate. The Pharisees understood "Sabbath" here to mean the first day of Unleavened Bread (a rest day, Nisan 15), so the sheaf was waved on Nisan 16. The Sadducees insisted it meant the weekly Sabbath within Passover week. The Pharisees' interpretation prevailed because, as Ellicott argues, if the weekly Sabbath could fall variably within the week, Pentecost would have no fixed reference point, "and the Passover itself would, in the course of time, be displaced from the fundamental position which it occupies" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)). Gill concurs: the "Sabbath" here is not the seventh-day Sabbath but "the first day of the feast of unleavened bread, which was a sabbath, in which no servile work was to be done" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html)).

Guzik notes the typological significance: "On the day after the Sabbath: This would be Sunday. 'Here the Lord's day was prefigured, saith one, therefore prescribed, and instituted of God' (Trapp)" ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

---

## v. 12: "On the day you wave the sheaf, you shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering…"

The accompanying burnt offering (a perfect yearling male lamb) typifies Christ. Gill: "Typical of the perfect and immaculate Lamb of God, whose sufferings are fitly signified by a burnt offering; and which were endured at the time he became the firstfruits of his people, and sanctified them" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html)).

---

## v. 13: "…its grain offering of two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour… and its drink offering of a quarter hin of wine."

The grain offering here was double the usual amount (normally one-tenth of an ephah; see Exodus 29:40). Ellicott says this doubling was "to exhibit the plentiful harvest" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)). Gill adds the theological point: "Thankfulness ought to be in proportion to mercies" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html)).

Two-tenths of an ephah is roughly 4 pounds (2 kg) of fine flour; a quarter hin of wine is roughly one quart or one litre (Guzik, [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

---

## v. 14: "You must not eat any bread or roasted or new grain until the very day you have brought this offering…"

No produce from the new harvest could be eaten until the firstfruits had been dedicated. Ellicott notes that "the unleavened bread for the first and the second days of Passover was prepared from the last year's harvest, but the bread for the following days could only be made from the new harvest after the formal dedication of it to the Lord" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

Sklar (Desiring God) observes the moral purpose: "Thankfulness is one of the first emotions to evaporate; this requirement made sure the Israelites gave proper thanksgiving and honor to their bountiful King before enjoying his generous provision (cf. Deuteronomy 26:10–11; Proverbs 3:9–10)" ([desiringgod.org/articles/israels-calendar-was-a-classroom](https://desiringgod.org/articles/israels-calendar-was-a-classroom)).

The command is a "permanent statute… wherever you live" — meaning it was binding throughout Israel's generations, not just at the sanctuary ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

---

## v. 15: "From the day after the Sabbath, the day you brought the sheaf of the wave offering, you are to count off seven full weeks."

This begins the countdown to Pentecost. "Seven sabbaths" (Hebrew) means seven complete weeks — 49 days. Ellicott explains: "The expression sabbath denotes here a week, hence the parallel passage substitutes the word week, viz., 'seven weeks shalt thou number unto thee' (Deuteronomy 16:9)" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)). The counting began from Nisan 16. Gill notes that the count began at evening, "or otherwise the weeks would not be complete" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-23.html)).

---

## v. 16: "You shall count off fifty days until the day after the seventh Sabbath, and then present an offering of new grain to the LORD."

The fiftieth day (Greek *pentekostos*, hence "Pentecost") was the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot). Ellicott: the fiftieth day could fall on Sivan 5, 6, or 7 (mid-May to mid-June). The "new grain offering" was of wheat — the later grain harvest — in contrast to the earlier barley firstfruits. Hence this is also called "the feast of harvest" (Exodus 23:16) because "it concluded the harvest of the later grain" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

Guzik notes the New Testament fulfilment: the name Pentecost is used in Acts 2:1 and Acts 20:16; the Holy Spirit was poured out on this very day, marking the birth of the Church ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

**Reformed/Presbyterian perspective:** Grant's Commentary (Brethren tradition) states that this feast "signifies in some sense a new beginning, for it was on this day (fifty days after the resurrection of Christ) that the Spirit of God came to indwell believers (Acts 2:1–47) and to begin the marvelous formation of the Church in unity on earth" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/leviticus-23.html)).

---

## v. 17: "Bring two loaves of bread from your dwellings as a wave offering… baked with leaven, as the firstfruits to the LORD."

The two loaves were made from two-tenths of an ephah of fine wheat flour each. Ellicott details their preparation: three seahs of new wheat were brought to the Temple court, beaten, trodden, ground, sifted with twelve sieves, kneaded with leaven into two loaves outside the Temple but baked inside. Each loaf was "seven hand-breadths long, four hand-breadths broad, and five fingers high" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

**Why leaven?** This is highly unusual because leaven was generally forbidden with blood offerings (Exodus 23:18; 34:25). The Expositor's Bible Commentary explains: unlike ordinary grain offerings, these loaves were "baked with leaven… because the offering was to represent the ordinary food of the people." They could not be placed on the altar because of the leaven, but were waved and then given to the priests ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/leviticus-23.html)).

Guzik sees a profound typology: the two leavened loaves represent Jew and Gentile brought together in the Church — sinful people (leaven) yet accepted before God through the accompanying blood sacrifices. "Remarkably, the Feast of Pentecost required two leavened loaves to be waved before the Lord — unusual since leaven was normally forbidden with blood offerings — symbolizing the bringing of Gentiles into God's covenant people" ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

---

## v. 18: "Along with the bread you are to present seven unblemished male lambs a year old, one young bull, and two rams…"

The animal sacrifices accompanying the wave loaves are distinct from the festival's own appointed sacrifices (Numbers 28:27 specifies two bullocks and one ram). Ellicott explains that "Those prescribed in Numbers were offered in the wilderness, whilst those prescribed here were only to be offered when the Israelites entered the Promised Land" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)). Poole notes that the variation between one bullock/two rams versus two bullocks/one ram left "it to their liberty to choose which they would offer" (quoted in Guzik, [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

---

## v. 19: "You shall also prepare one male goat as a sin offering and two male lambs a year old as a peace offering."

The sin offering (purification offering) dealt with impurity, and the peace offering expressed fellowship and thanksgiving. Together with the burnt offerings, this covered the full range of sacrificial worship: dedication (burnt), purification (sin), and communion (peace) ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

---

## v. 20: "The priest is to wave the lambs as a wave offering before the LORD, together with the bread of the firstfruits. The bread and the two lambs shall be holy to the LORD for the priest."

Ellicott describes the temple ritual: the two lambs were waved while still alive, then slain. The priest took the breast and shoulder of each (see Leviticus 7:30–32), laid them beside the two loaves, put both hands underneath, and waved them "towards the east side forwards and backwards, up and down." The fat was burned; the rest was the priests' portion. Of the two loaves, the high priest took one and the other was divided among officiating priests, to be eaten within the same day and half the following night ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

---

## v. 21: "On that same day you are to proclaim a sacred assembly, and you must not do any regular work…"

Like the other major feasts, Pentecost was a day of holy convocation and rest from servile work. The proclamation was made "by the priest with trumpet blasts" (Ellicott). By the second Temple period, this day was also regarded as the anniversary of the giving of the Law at Sinai, and "the Israelites to this day sacredly keep this festival on the 6th and 7th of Sivan" with synagogues and homes adorned with flowers and greenery ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

Grant's Commentary also emphasizes the grace character: "customary (or servile) work was forbidden, for Pentecost speaks of another great work of God in which people are blessed by God's grace without any work on their part" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/leviticus-23.html)).

---

## v. 22: "When you reap the harvest of your land, do not reap all the way to the edges… Leave them for the poor and the foreign resident. I am the LORD your God."

This repeats the command of Leviticus 19:9–10. Ellicott observes: "In the midst of rejoicing and thankfulness to God for a bountiful harvest, the Lawgiver again inculcates the duty of remembering the poor, and reminds the proprietors of the land that the needy have legally a share in the produce" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

Guzik notes this was an appropriate reminder right after the law concerning the harvest feast of Pentecost: gratitude to God must overflow in generosity to others ([enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)).

Grant's Commentary draws a dispensational application: "being the recipients of God's grace today, we should show the same grace to others, as Galatians 2:10 insists. As well as this, the grace of God by which we have been so greatly blessed, will not be exhausted when the Church is translated to heaven: there will be abundance of grace left for the poor of Israel and for stranger Gentiles who will be brought to God during the tribulation period" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/leviticus-23.html)).

Sklar (Desiring God / Reformed) sees the repetition of this law at Pentecost as teaching "the value that [God] puts on compassion and care for others. Maximizing personal profit is not the highest priority for Yahweh followers. Caring for fellow image-bearers is" ([desiringgod.org/articles/israels-calendar-was-a-classroom](https://desiringgod.org/articles/israels-calendar-was-a-classroom)).

---

## Summary of Traditional Typological Reading (agreed across most Protestant traditions)

| Feast | OT Meaning | NT Fulfilment |
|---|---|---|
| Passover (v. 5) | Deliverance from Egypt by the lamb's blood | Christ our Passover Lamb (1 Cor 5:7) — His death |
| Unleavened Bread (vv. 6–8) | Purity; removal of leaven | Christ's sinless burial; call to holy living (1 Cor 5:7–8) |
| Firstfruits (vv. 9–14) | First sheaf of barley harvest, waved on "the day after the Sabbath" | Christ's resurrection as "firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Cor 15:20) |
| Pentecost / Weeks (vv. 15–21) | Wheat harvest; two leavened loaves waved | Descent of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2); birth of the Church incorporating Jew and Gentile |

---

## Denominational Differences and Other Views Noted

**1. The "Sabbath" in vv. 11, 15 — Sadducees vs. Pharisees:** The Sadducees took "Sabbath" literally (the weekly Sabbath during Passover week); the Pharisees took it as the first day of Unleavened Bread (Nisan 15, a rest day). Jewish tradition and most Christian commentators follow the Pharisaic interpretation, which makes the day after "Sabbath" consistently Nisan 16 and anchors Pentecost 50 days later. Ellicott provides the fullest discussion of this from among the sources fetched ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-23.html)).

**2. The Sabbath and the Lord's Day (v. 3):** As noted above, the main Protestant divide concerns whether the Sabbath command continues as a binding moral law transferred to Sunday (Lutheran, some Reformed, some Anglican), or whether it is entirely fulfilled in Christ so that no particular day is required (mainstream Reformed/Baptist, as articulated by Guzik at Enduring Word). Peake's Commentary (modern critical) notes that "The term 'set feast' (RV) means 'an assembly'… The older name for these feasts was *hag*, properly a pilgrimage; this term, however, would not apply to the Sabbath" ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-23.html)).

**3. Modern critical scholarship (Peake's Commentary):** Peake regards the chapter as composite — "considerably expanded by a later priestly writer." The original sections referred only to the three great feasts (Unleavened Bread, Weeks, Ingathering). Evidence includes "the new commencement in Leviticus 23:9, the repetition of Leviticus 19:9 in Leviticus 23:22, the reference to Leviticus 16:30 in Leviticus 23:26 ff., and the parallel sections in Leviticus 23:33 ff. and Leviticus 23:39 ff." In the analysis, H (the Holiness Code) emphasizes agriculture, while P (Priestly writer) emphasizes rest, assembly at the sanctuary, and set sacrifice ([studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-23.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-23.html)).
